technique: scale — moving between the tiny and the large in a few lines
lesson:
Today we work on one move: scale. Scale means the poem shifts between something small and something large within a few lines.

Watch where the poem goes from tiny to wide. It starts with "a small ache there," a spot inside your own mouth. Then it moves out to "the long lawn down the slope." Then it moves further out to "Light's coming up behind the ridge."

Here is why that works on you mechanically. When the size of what you look at changes fast, your attention has to reset each time. You feel the ache, then you pull back to see a whole lawn, then a whole ridge. The jump makes the small thing feel connected to the large thing. You notice both more than if the poem stayed one size.

Try this: in three lines, name one thing the size of your hand, then one thing the size of a yard, then one thing the size of the sky.

The second time through, track how far out your eye travels before the poem says "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
A crow starts up somewhere past the treeline,
one rough note, then quiet, like it thought better of the hour.
You lie a minute in that hush and take the measure of your mouth—
a small ache there, a thing that wants a word with you come winter,
the body sending word ahead the way the frost does.
Let it keep. The jar of garlic's waiting on the sill,
each clove a little promise you can set by hand into the dark,
and the long lawn down the slope stands sandy, thin, forgiving,
ready for whatever you choose to make it carry.
Light's coming up behind the ridge now, pale and plain as water.
You've got hours to spend and the strength to spend them well.

Cold ground's holding a place for what you'll tuck in before the freeze—and there's music to chase down the road besides—

So — up!
